annotations.text:
WHY THIS EXISTS

20 November 2026: the panel came up on the living room TV, plugged into the hub, and stopped at the passcode. A screen joining a house with a passcode is asked for it (design/companion/, C), and on a TV only a keyboard could type it: the remote's number buttons are switched off, so 1 to 4 never start a scene by accident. Above it, the first-start pill asked to be tapped to turn the screen over.

THE SAME IN EVERY DIRECTION

NO PILL ON A TV. A TV is never hung upside down and has no glass to tap, so the first-start pill is not drawn there. This screen keeps the four ways up for anybody who needs them.

ASKING A PHONE IS ALWAYS THERE. Any phone already in the house can say yes, the way a second wall screen joins today.

READ FROM THE SOFA. Nothing a person must read is under 22px, something is always lit, and the line at the foot says what each key does.

Only on a TV. A phone and the wall join exactly as they do today.

A: THE REMOTE'S NUMBER BUTTONS

The passcode is four digits, and most TV remotes have the ten buttons that type them. On this screen they type; everywhere else the colored buttons stay the scenes, and the digits do nothing.

The quickest for the person holding the remote, and the screen stays as it is, only bigger.

AGAINST: some remotes have no number buttons (a few new ones, most USB air mice), and then the only way in is asking a phone.

Try it: type four digits, Escape takes one off.

B: A KEYPAD THE ARROWS MOVE ON

Twelve cards beside the question: the digits, one that takes a digit off, and Join. The arrows and OK work every remote there is, and the number buttons still type straight in where a remote has them.

The way every TV app asks for a PIN, so it is familiar.

AGAINST: slower with arrows only, about a dozen presses for four digits, and the pad is a second thing to draw on a screen people see once.

Try it: arrows and Enter, or type digits.

C: THE HUB'S OWN TV IS ALREADY IN

The TV plugged into the hub is the hub's own glass: the hub already knows that request comes from itself (it is how only that screen is shown the hub's Wi-Fi password, design/screen-wifi/). So it is let in without a passcode and asked only which room it is in.

A TV on another box, which is where somebody could plug in a stranger's, asks the phones in the house first, with B's keypad behind Type the passcode instead.

FOR: the TV people will set up most is a Hub Plus on the living room TV, and it never asks. AGAINST: anyone who can reach the hub's HDMI port gets in without the passcode. They could already restart or reset it from there, but it is a rule the wall does not have today.

PICK ONE

A, B or C, a mix (C's own TV with A's digits elsewhere, say), or something else -- describe it.
